sentences.text: The genus Zuolong was formally established by Choiniere and colleagues in 2010.
Its name combines the Chinese word for dragon with the surname of General Zuo Zongtang, a historical figure who secured the Xinjiang region for China.
The type species designated for this genus is Zuolong salleei.
The holotype, which serves as the primary specimen for the species, is cataloged as IVPP V15912 and contains a partially complete skull along with numerous post-cranial bones.
The skull exhibits a triangular shape with a snout that narrows considerably toward the tip.
Distinctive features include very large eye sockets facing the sides and a lacrimal bone process that formed a small crest above the eyes.
In life, the animal possessed four premaxillary and twelve maxillary teeth, which were D-shaped in cross-section, a trait shared with tyrannosauroids but less convex than in those groups.
The preserved skeleton includes twenty-two vertebrae representing all four vertebral segments.
The manual claws are strongly curved and feature lateral grooves running along their length.
The hip bones display a supraacetabular crest extending from the rear end of the acetabulum.
Gregory S. Paul hypothesized that the holotype is a juvenile and estimated an adult length of 3 meters and a mass of 50 kg.
Some authors suggest an adult Zuolong reached a length of 3.35 meters and a mass of 43 kg.
In 2016, Gregory S. Paul estimated Zuolong's length at 3 meters and its weight at 60 kilograms.
The fossil was found in the upper part of the Shishugou Formation near Wucaiwan in Xinjiang, China.
Although the specimen was discovered in 2001, it remained unpublished until 2010.
The formal description was published by Jonah Choiniere, James Clark, Catherine Forester, and Xu Xing.
The specific name salleei honors Hilmar Sallee, whose donation helped finance the research.
Thomas R. Holtz Jr. considers the holotype specimen to almost certainly belong to a juvenile theropod.
The holotype was a subadult individual measuring approximately 3.1 meters in length and weighing up to 35 kilograms.
The most common hypothesis regarding Zuolong's taxonomy is that it is a basal member of Coelurosauria.
In 2019, it was discovered that Zuolong was a member of Tyrannoraptora in a polytomy with Tyrannosauroidea and Maniraptoromorpha.

Subsequent studies, including a 2020 description of Aratasaurus, a 2022 phylogeny by Rolando and colleagues, and a 2024 study by Andrea Cau, have included Zuolong in their analyses of coelurosaur relationships.
Zuolong lived during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic period, between 161 and 155 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
The specific age of the holotype specimen is estimated between 161.2 and 155.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether the implications of Zuolong's discovery as one of the oldest known coelurosaurs can be fully understood without more fossil material.
Xing and colleagues suggest that the discrepancy between their ontogeny and conventional analyses highlights the need for more specimens to confidently establish phylogenetic relationships.
